theory.title: Encapsulation & Access Modifiers
theory.summary: Classes are the foundation of Object-Oriented Programming in C++. They allow you to bundle data and the functions that operate on that data into a single unit.
bullets: Private: Members only accessible within the class itself (Data Hiding).
Public: Members accessible from anywhere the object is visible.
Methods: Functions defined inside a class that operate on its private state.

theory.title: Struct vs Class
theory.summary: In C++, the only technical difference between a struct and a class is the default access level. Structs are 'public' by default, while classes are 'private' by default.
bullets: POD (Plain Old Data): Structs are often used for simple groupings of variables.
Public Access: Ideal for components where encapsulation isn't required.
Memory Layout: Variables are typically stored in the order they are declared.

interactive_questions.title: Generic Logic with Templates
interactive_questions.question: See how Templates allow you to write logic that works with any data type.
interactive_questions.explanation: Templates are a key part of C++ Meta-programming, allowing the compiler to generate specialized versions of a function for different types.

theory.title: The Power of Templates
theory.summary: Templates enable 'Generic Programming'. Instead of writing different functions for int, float, and double, you write one template and the compiler does the rest.
bullets: Compile-time Generation: Templates don't exist at runtime; the compiler generates the code you need.
Type Safety: Unlike void pointers, templates are fully type-checked by the compiler.
STL: The entire Standard Template Library (vectors, maps) is built on this foundation.

steps.title: Type Parameterization
steps.description: The 'template <typename T>' declares that T is a placeholder for a type that will be decided when the function is used.

mcq.question: What does 'T' represent in this code?

options.reasoning: T is a generic type name, not a variable.

options.text: A placeholder that can represent int, float, or even custom types.
options.reasoning: T (Type) allows the function to be polymorphic based on the arguments provided.

steps.title: Template Deduction
steps.description: In many cases, the compiler can 'deduce' the type T from the arguments, so you don't always have to write <int> explicitly.

mcq.question: How does the compiler handle the call 'getMax(5.5f, 2.1f)'?

options.text: It generates a version of the function where T is replaced with 'float'.
options.reasoning: This process is called Template Instantiation.

options.text: It converts 5.5f to an integer and uses the integer version.
options.reasoning: Templates preserve the original types to ensure precision and type safety.

interactive_questions.question: Scroll to understand how std::vector dynamically manages memory.
interactive_questions.explanation: std::vector is a dynamic array that handles resizing automatically by reallocating memory when its capacity is reached.

theory.title: Dynamic Arrays via std::vector
theory.summary: Vectors are sequence containers representing arrays that can change in size.
bullets: Contiguous Memory: Elements are stored sequentially, providing fast O(1) random access.
Capacity vs. Size: Size is how many elements exist; capacity is how much space is allocated.
Reallocation: When size exceeds capacity, the vector typically doubles its capacity, copying old elements.

steps.title: Initialization
steps.description: An empty vector is created. At this point, it usually hasn't allocated any heap memory, so its size and capacity are both 0.

options.reasoning: The vector is empty, so accessing index 0 goes out of bounds.

options.reasoning: Vectors do not automatically pad empty indexes unless pre-allocated.

steps.title: Growth Rate
steps.description: $snippet push_back() snippet$ appends elements. If the new size exceeds capacity, the vector allocates a larger chunk of memory (often doubling), copies elements, and deletes the old chunk.

mcq.question: Which snippet accurately represents pre-allocating memory to avoid these expensive reallocations?

options.text: $snippet numbers.resize(5); snippet$
options.reasoning: Resize also changes the actual size and constructs elements. $snippet reserve() snippet$ only changes capacity.

options.text: $snippet numbers.reserve(5); snippet$

steps.title: Reclaiming Memory
steps.description: Vectors rarely reduce their capacity automatically when elements are removed. $snippet shrink_to_fit() snippet$ requests the container to reduce its capacity to fit its size.

mcq.question: Is $snippet shrink_to_fit() snippet$ guaranteed to reduce capacity?

options.text: Yes, it forces the vector to drop excess memory immediately.
options.reasoning: It's technically a non-binding request; the implementation might ignore it for optimization reasons.

options.text: No, it's a non-binding request to the implementations' allocator.

theory.title: Variadic Templates & Parameter Packs
theory.summary: Sometimes you don't know how many arguments a function will receive (like a smart pointer maker or a custom print function). Variadic templates solve this type-safely.
bullets: Parameter Pack: Declared using an ellipsis `...`, represents zero or more parameters.
Recursive Unpacking: You process arguments by popping off the first one, then recursively calling the function with the rest.
Compile-Time: All recursion happens at compile time, leading to highly optimized code.

steps.title: The Parameter Pack
steps.description: $snippet typename... Args snippet$ defines a template parameter pack. $snippet Args... rest snippet$ defines a function parameter pack. It captures any number of additional arguments.

mcq.question: What are the types captured in $snippet Args snippet$ during the first call $snippet printAll(10, "Hello", 3.14, 'A') snippet$?

options.text: $snippet const char*, double, char snippet$
options.reasoning: T is deduced as int for the first argument (10). Args captures the remaining types.

options.text: $snippet int, const char*, double, char snippet$
options.reasoning: The first argument satisfies 'T', so 'Args' only contains the subsequent elements.

steps.title: Pack Expansion
steps.description: To use the pack, we apply the $snippet ... snippet$ operator. $snippet printAll(rest...) snippet$ unpacks the remaining arguments into the next function call.

mcq.question: What is the primary mechanism variadic templates use to process arguments in C++11?

options.text: Compile-time recursion generating a new function signature for each step.
options.reasoning: The compiler creates a chain of function overloads decreasing in argument count.

options.text: A runtime loop iterating over an array of `std::any`.
options.reasoning: Templates are evaluated strictly at compile-time.

steps.title: The Base Case
steps.description: Because the expansion relies on recursion, we need an empty function to handle the final call when the parameter pack is entirely empty.

interactive_questions.title: std::deque: The Ring Buffer
interactive_questions.question: Scroll to learn how a double-ended queue balances fast access with efficient insertions.
interactive_questions.explanation: std::deque (double-ended queue) is not a single contiguous block of memory like std::vector, but a sequence of fixed-size arrays.

theory.title: Understanding std::deque (Deck)
theory.summary: While std::vector is great for appending, front-insertions are slow (O(n)). std::deque offers fast O(1) insertions at both the front and back.
bullets: Segmented Memory: Internally, it manages a 'map' (array of pointers) pointing to fixed-size memory blocks.
No Reallocation Copies: Adding elements to the front or back doesn't require copying existing elements to a new array.
Random Access: Like vector, you can quickly access any index, but math is slightly more complex across boundaries.

steps.title: Front Insertions
steps.description: In a $snippet std::vector snippet$, $snippet push_front() snippet$ does not exist because shifting all elements right costs O(n). In $snippet std::deque snippet$, it's an O(1) operation.

mcq.question: How does $snippet std::deque snippet$ achieve O(1) front insertions without shifting elements?

options.text: It allocates memory in separate chunks, and prepends a new chunk if the first one is full.
options.reasoning: The deque uses an array of pointers to fixed-size arrays, allowing O(1) growth in both directions.

options.text: It shifts the memory start pointer backwards into free space.
options.reasoning: Contiguous sequences can't guarantee there's free space 'before' the array block.

steps.title: Random Access
steps.description: Despite being fragmented, $snippet std::deque snippet$ allows direct access to elements using the $snippet [] snippet$ operator.

mcq.question: Why is $snippet dq[2] snippet$ slightly slower in a deque compared to a vector?

options.text: Vectors use simple pointer offset math. Deques require two lookups: finding the target chunk, then the offset inside it.
options.reasoning: Correct! Deque math involves dividing by chunk size to find the block pointer, then using modulo for the exact element.

options.text: Because it has to iterate from the head node to the third node like a linked list.
options.reasoning: std::deque is NOT a linked list (like `std::list`), it offers true random access.

steps.title: Back Insertions
steps.description: Just like a vector, pushing to the back is fast. But unlike a vector, pushing elements never invalidates pointers to existing elements.

mcq.question: Which snippet accurately represents when you should favor $snippet std::vector snippet$ over $snippet std::deque snippet$?

options.text: When you need strict contiguous memory (e.g. interfacing with C-APIs using $snippet &vec[0] snippet$).
options.reasoning: Because a deque is chunked, you cannot pass its underlying array to an API expecting a contiguous buffer.

options.text: When you need to insert elements at both ends frequently.
options.reasoning: That is the exact use-case intended for `std::deque` over `std::vector`.
